extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students in probability theory or readers of a probability textbook
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Poisson processes, compound Poisson constructions, thinning and conditioning results, and the theory of stable laws and infinitely divisible distributions including limit theorems and characteristic-function representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poisson limit for sums of rare events (Theorem 3.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X_{n,m}, 1 ≤ m ≤ n be independent nonnegative integer-valued r.v.'s with P(X_{n,m}=1)=p_{n,m}, P(X_{n,m}≥2)=ε_{n,m}. If (i) sum_{m=1}^n p_{n,m} → λ ∈ (0,∞), (ii) max_{1≤m≤n} p_{n,m} → 0, and (iii) sum_{m=1}^n ε_{n,m} → 0, then S_n = Σ_{m=1}^n X_{n,m} ⇒ Poisson(λ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: approximate by Bernoulli( p_{n,m} ) indicators (throw away events with ≥2 occurrences), use Theorem 3.6.1 (Poisson limit for sums of Bernoulli's) and the 'converging together' lemma. Conditions ensure rare, approximately independent single occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poisson counts from small-interval assumptions (Theorem 3.7.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For arrival counts N(s,t) assume (i) numbers in disjoint intervals independent, (ii) distribution depends only on interval length t−s (stationary increments), (iii) P(N(0,h)=1)=λh+o(h), and (iv) P(N(0,h)≥2)=o(h). Then N(0,t) ~ Poisson(λt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via partitioning [0,t] into many small intervals, letting X_{n,m}=N((m−1)t/n, mt/n) and applying Theorem 3.7.1. The o(h) conditions capture rarity of multiple arrivals in infinitesimal intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Poisson process (rate λ)
rubrics_metrics.description: A family {N(t), t≥0} is a Poisson process with rate λ if (i) for 0=t_0< t_1<...<t_n the increments N(t_k)−N(t_{k−1}) are independent, and (ii) N(t)−N(s) ∼ Poisson(λ(t−s)) for s<t (stationary independent increments with Poisson law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative constructive characterization: exponential interarrival times produce the same process. This definition is the basis for many properties (independent increments, distributional formulas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction from exponential interarrival times
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ξ_i be i.i.d. with P(ξ_i > t) = e^{−λt} (exponential(λ)). Set T_n = ξ_1 + ... + ξ_n and N_t = sup{n : T_n ≤ t}. Then N_t is a Poisson process with rate λ (counts are Poisson(λt) and increments independent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Erlang density for T_n, calculations showing P(N_t = n) = e^{−λt}(λt)^n/n!. Also shows independence of counts on disjoint intervals via memoryless property of exponential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memoryless property of the exponential distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: P(T > t+s | T > t) = P(T > s) for exponential random variable T (lack-of-memory property).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key fact used to show that arrivals after time t are independent of history before time t and have the same exponential distribution for waiting time to next arrival; central to proving independent increments of the constructed process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wald's identity and variance for random sums (Theorem 3.7.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Y_i i.i.d., N independent nonnegative integer r.v., and S = Σ_{i=1}^N Y_i with S=0 when N=0. (i) If E|Y_i|, E N < ∞ then E S = E N · E Y_i (Wald's equation). (ii) If E Y_i^2, E N^2 < ∞ then Var(S) = E N · Var(Y_i) + Var(N)·(E Y_i)^2. (iii) If N ∼ Poisson(λ), then Var(S) = λ E Y_i^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by conditioning on N: compute E(S|N=n) and E(S^2|N=n) and average. The variance decomposition separates contribution from variability of individual summands and variability in the number of summands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thinning of Poisson processes (Theorem 3.7.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a Poisson(λ) process where each arrival is independently labeled with value Y_i, define N_j(t) = number of arrivals by time t with Y_i = j. Then each N_j(t) is an independent Poisson process with rate λ·P(Y_i = j).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via multinomial splitting of counts in an interval: conditioned on total arrivals, the counts by type are multinomial; marginally each type is Poisson and different types are independent. Intuition: random thinning yields independent Poisson subprocesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonhomogeneous thinning (Theorem 3.7.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If in a Poisson process with (possibly time-varying) rate λ(s) we independently keep each point occurring at time s with probability p(s), then the retained points form a (nonhomogeneous) Poisson process with rate λ(s) p(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalizes constant-rate thinning. Used in applications (e.g., modeling selective retention or filtering over time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poisson process on a measure space (Example 3.7.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Poisson process on (S, 𝒮, μ) is a random measure m such that for disjoint sets A_i with μ(A_i)<∞, the counts m(A_i) are independent and Poisson with mean μ(A_i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction for finite-mean measure: draw N ∼ Poisson(μ(S)) and place N iid points in S with law ν = μ/μ(S); extend to infinite measure by partitioning space. μ is called the mean measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional distribution of arrival times given count (Theorem 3.7.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix t and let T_1,...,T_n be arrival times of the first n arrivals in a rate-λ Poisson process. Conditioned on N(t)=n, the unordered arrival times are distributed as n i.i.d. Uniform(0,t) order statistics; i.e., the vector of ordered arrival times has the same distribution as the order statistics of n independent Uniform(0,t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute joint density of T_1,...,T_n conditional on N(t)=n and compare to joint density of order statistics of uniforms; yields convenient conditioning formulas and corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial conditional distribution of counts (Corollary 3.7.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: For 0 < s < t, P(N(s)=m | N(t)=n) = C(n,m) (s/t)^m (1 − s/t)^{n−m}, i.e., conditional split of n arrivals over [0,s] and (s,t] is Binomial(n, s/t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate consequence of arrival times conditioned being uniform order statistics; useful for conditional inference and thinning arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalized arrival times have uniform order-statistics law (Theorem 3.7.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a rate-λ Poisson process, condition on N(t)=n and let T_{n+1} be time of (n+1)-th arrival; then (T_1/T_{n+1}, ..., T_n/T_{n+1}) has the same distribution as the order statistics of n independent Uniform(0,1) variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses change of variables and Jacobian calculation; useful for spacing and empirical-process style results. Leads to spacings limit theorems in exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacings and extremes of uniform order statistics (exercises 3.7.6–3.7.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of exercises relate spacings between order statistics of i.i.d. Uniforms to limit theorems (e.g., scaled maxima, minimum spacings converge in distribution or probability to exponential or other limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are applications of Theorem 3.7.11 and classical limit results; referenced results include Smirnov (1949), Weiss (1955) and laws for maxima/minima spacing behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain of attraction conditions for stable laws (Theorem 3.8.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X_i i.i.d. satisfy (i) tail balance lim_{x→∞} P(X_1 > x)/P(|X_1| > x) = θ ∈ [0,1], and (ii) P(|X_1| > x) = x^{−α} L(x) where 0<α<2 and L is slowly varying. Define a_n = inf{ x : P(|X_1| > x) ≤ 1/n } and b_n = n E(X_1 1_{|X_1| ≤ a_n}). Then (S_n − b_n)/a_n ⇒ Y where Y is nondegenerate (a stable law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions are essentially necessary and sufficient for convergence of normalized sums to a stable law. The theorem describes how to choose scaling a_n and centering b_n and links tail behavior to index α and asymmetry parameter θ; proof uses Poisson point process limits of large jumps and truncation arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: slowly varying function
rubrics_metrics.description: A measurable function L is slowly varying if for all t>0, lim_{x→∞} L(tx)/L(x) = 1 (e.g., L(x)=log x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slow variation is used to describe tails of distributions that are regularly varying up to a slowly varying factor; central in domain-of-attraction characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection lemma for double-limits (Lemma 3.8.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If h_n(ε) → g(ε) for each ε>0 and g(ε)→g(0) as ε→0, then one can pick ε_n→0 so that h_n(ε_n) → g(0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A technical but frequently used diagonalization lemma to produce a sequence of truncation thresholds ε_n→0 that realizes desired double-limit behavior; used in truncation/summation proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tail comparison bound for regularly varying tails (Lemma 3.8.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given P(|X|>x)=x^{−α}L(x) with slowly varying L and any δ>0, there exists C such that for all t≥t_0 and y≤1, P(|X|>yt)/P(|X|>t) ≤ C y^{−α−δ}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify dominated convergence/interchange of integrals in truncation arguments; gives a uniform power-law bound with slack δ to control small-y behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic function representation of stable laws (formula 3.8.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stable law characteristic functions can be written as exp(i t c − b |t|^α (1 + i κ sgn(t) w_α(t))) where −1 ≤ κ ≤ 1 (κ=2θ−1) and w_α(t)=tan(πα/2) for α≠1 and (2/π) log|t| for α=1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formula identifies parameters: index α, scale b, location c, skewness κ; special cases: α=2 gives normal (κ term vanishes), α=1, κ=0 is Cauchy, α=1/2, κ=1 gives an explicit positive-stable density. The representation follows from the Poisson-sum / truncation derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable laws defined via stability under summation
rubrics_metrics.description: A random variable Y has a stable law if for every integer k>0 there exist constants a_k>0, b_k such that for i.i.d. copies Y_1,...,Y_k with same law as Y, (Y_1+...+Y_k − b_k)/a_k has the same distribution as Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property characterizes stable distributions; Theorem 3.8.8 links this definition to limits of normalized sums of i.i.d. variables (domain of attraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable laws are exactly limits of normalized sums (Theorem 3.8.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: A distribution Y is the limit of (X_1+...+X_n − b_n)/a_n for some i.i.d. sequence X_i if and only if Y has a stable law (i.e., is stable under convolution up to location/scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs block-sums and uses stability under grouping to show limit law must be stable; conversely a stable law trivially arises as limit by taking X_i i.i.d. with law Y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence-of-types theorem (Theorem 3.8.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If W_n ⇒ W and there exist α_n>0, β_n with α_n W_n + β_n ⇒ W' where W and W' are nondegenerate limits, then α_n → α and β_n → β for some finite α, β (i.e., centering/scaling sequences converge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem prevents pathological oscillations of norming constants in limit theorems; proof uses characteristic-function arguments and tightness of point-mass sequences arising from the β_n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples illustrating domains of attraction and scaling (various examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple worked examples: (i) reciprocals of symmetric continuous density at 0 give Cauchy limit (α=1, κ=0); (ii) hitting-time sums produce α=1/2 stable law; (iii) net force from random points in [−n,n] leads to index 1/p; (iv) explicit centering behavior depending on α (α<1 centering negligible, α>1 centering ∼ nμ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show how tail behavior and symmetry/asymmetry determine index α, skew κ, scaling a_n and centering b_n; they illustrate how to verify hypotheses of Theorem 3.8.2 in concrete settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitely divisible limit characterization (Theorem 3.9.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A distribution Z is a limit of triangular-array sums S_n = Σ_{m=1}^n X_{n,m} (with X_{n,m} i.i.d. within rows) if and only if Z is infinitely divisible (for each n there exist i.i.d. components adding to Z in distribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessity proof: split S_{2n} into two independent equal-distribution sums, extract subsequential limits to show Z decomposes into sum of independent identically distributed pieces; sufficiency is by construction of triangular arrays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound Poisson characteristic function formula (Example 3.9.5 / equation 3.9.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Z = Σ_{i=1}^{N(λ)} ξ_i with N(λ) ∼ Poisson(λ) independent of i.i.d. ξ_i with ch.f. ϕ(t), then E e^{itZ} = exp(−λ(1 − ϕ(t))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows compound Poisson laws are infinitely divisible; explains how normal and stable laws can be obtained as limits of compound Poisson distributions by letting jump distribution and rate vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lévy–Khinchin representation for infinitely divisible distributions (Theorem 3.9.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A distribution is infinitely divisible iff its characteristic function ϕ satisfies log ϕ(t) = i c t − (σ^2 t^2)/2 + ∫_{ℝ} (e^{itx} − 1 − (itx)/(1+x^2)) μ(dx), where μ is a Lévy measure (μ({0})=0 and ∫ x^2/(1+x^2) μ(dx) < ∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This canonical decomposition separates Gaussian part (σ^2), drift (c), and jump structure via the Lévy measure μ; integrability condition ensures finite behaviour near 0 and infers many structural properties of infinitely divisible laws.
